project_name: Monte Carlo Simulations: From calculating area to Gambling in BlackJack
project_description: This five-week project is a structured journey designed to take you from a programming novice to the architect of a simple artificial intelligence. We begin in the first week by building a solid foundation, mastering the essential computational toolkit of Python and its numerical library, NumPy. With these tools in hand, our second week is dedicated to building a deep and intuitive understanding of the Monte Carlo method; we will write a simulation to estimate the areas of complex geometric shapes by metaphorically throwing millions of virtual darts, discovering how random sampling can be used to solve problems that would otherwise require calculus. Armed with this practical foundation in simulation, we then pause in the third week to learn the core theoretical language of Reinforcement Learning, defining the abstract concepts of agents, environments, policies, and value functions that are the building blocks of intelligent systems. In the fourth week, we bridge this theory with practice by applying our Monte Carlo skills to the game of Blackjack, not to play it, but to build an analytical engine that can evaluate any given strategy by calculating the long-term value of every possible game situation. Finally, in the culminating week, we empower our agent to learn for itself, implementing a Monte Carlo Control algorithm that allows it to start with zero knowledge, learn from the outcomes of thousands of games, and independently discover the mathematically optimal strategy to play Blackjack, completing the transformation from simple simulation to genuine artificial intelligence.

project_name: Beyond the blackbox
mentor_name: Tanishk nath goswami, Farhan al zayed
project_description:
This course is for students who know how to call model.fit() but want to understand what is happening under the hood. We will mathematically derive the "why" behind model behavior, optimization, and generalization, using linear algebra and calculus skills as our primary tool

In the first week, we will cover the core tradeoff in all of machine learning. We'll move beyond the vague idea of overfitting and formalize it. The session will introduce the statistical learning framework, distinguishing between the empirical risk (training error) and the true risk (test error). The main discussion topic will be the Bias-Variance Decomposition, breaking down the test error into its three conceptual parts: bias, which results from a model's overly simplistic assumptions; variance, which results from the model's sensitivity to the specific training data it saw; and irreducible error. This framework provides the core language for discussing why a simple model is stable but wrong (high bias, low variance) and a complex model is accurate but sensitive (low bias, high variance).

For the second week, the topic is optimization and the cost landscape, exploring how a model learns. We will frame learning as an optimization problem: finding the minimum of a high-dimensional cost function. Using linear algebra, we can represent the cost function, such as Mean SquaredError, in matrix form. The discussion will then compare the two primary methods for solving this. First, the analytical, one-shot solution given by the Normal Equation, which requires matrix inversion. Second, the iterative solution of Gradient Descent. The core of the discussion will be the computational tradeoffs between these two methods, explaining why the Normal Equation is often infeasible for high-dimensional data, which makes scalable algorithms like Stochastic Gradient Descent the workhorse of modern machine learning.

Week three will focus on generalization and model complexity, answering the question, Why does a model work on data it hasn't seen? We will discuss the need for a rigorous measure of model complexity that goes beyond just counting parameters. This leads to the central concept of VC Dimension, which we will explore intuitively through the idea of shattering. A model class's expressiveness, its VC dim, is the maximum number of points it can perfectly classify, regardless of how they are labeled. The key illustrative example for this session will be a walkthrough of why a 2D linear classifier can shatter any 3 points, but cannot shatter 4 points arranged in an XOR configuration, thus proving its complexity is finite even if the number of possible lines is infinite.

In week four, we will discuss the practical tools for controlling complexity, which are based on the theories from the previous weeks. The first part of the session will cover L2 (Ridge) and L1 (Lasso) regularization. We will use the linear algebra background to frame these as penalties on the vector norm of the model's weights. The discussion will center on the geometric intuition: the L2 norm's circle constraint shrinks all weights, while the L1 norm's diamond constraint has sharp corners that can force weights to exactly zero, thus performing feature selection. The second part of the session will cover the Kernel Trick, the conceptual magic behind models like SVMs, which allows us to solve non-linear problems by mapping data to a much higher-dimensional space where it becomes linearly separable, all without ever paying the computational cost of that transformation.

The final week will serve as a capstone, discussing the modern paradox of deep learning and where classical theory breaks. We will present the central mystery of deep learning: these models are massively over-parameterized, with far more parameters than data points. According to classical VC theory, they should overfit completely, but they generalize extremely well. This session will introduce the Double Descent phenomenon, where test error can surprisingly decrease again after passing the point of interpolation. This leads to the modern research topic of implicit regularization, suggesting the optimization algorithm itself is providing a hidden bias toward simpler solutions that our classical theories do not fully capture, making it a live and active field of research.
prerequisites: Basic python, enthu, basics of linear algebra(soft pre req)

project_name: Quant Agents: A Game Theory Model
project_description:
Have you ever wondered why stock markets crash or why "bubbles" form? Is it driven by complex calculations, or just simple crowd psychology? In this project, we'll build an artificial stock market from the ground up to find the answer.

This project involves building an artificial stock market from scratch using Agent-Based Modeling (ABM). We will simulate a market populated by 100 autonomous "Quant Agents" whose interactions are governed by a core Game Theory rule: the Minority Game.

In this game, agents profit only by being in the minority (e.g., selling when the majority buys). Agents are not static; they are adaptive. Each agent possesses a "toolbox" of 10 unique trading strategies (heuristics) and maintains a "scorebook" tracking the virtual performance of each.
At each time step, an agent deploys the strategy with the currently highest score. This creates a non-stationary environment: as a strategy becomes popular, it becomes the majority and thus unprofitable, forcing agents to adapt. This dynamic feedback loop allows us to study the emergent behavior of a complex system, such as market oscillations and volatility clustering.

You will learn to:
• Implement a multi-agent simulation in Python using the Mesa framework.
• Model adaptive agents using heuristic scoring mechanisms.
• Analyze the emergent, collective dynamics of a market from simple, individual rules.
• Apply concepts from Game Theory and Econophysics to financial data.
prerequisites: Common sense, Python, Basics of ML like regression

project_name: Sentiment Analysis for Social Media Posts
project_description:
This project is a complete tool built to analyze and automatically classify the sentiment of social media posts. The system processes a large volume of raw text and uses a Natural Language Processing (NLP) pipeline to accurately categorize each post as Positive, Negative, or Neutral.

Project Pipeline & Features:
1. Real-World Data Cleaning: The system is designed to handle "noisy" text from social media. It includes a robust cleaning module that automatically removes URLs, hashtags (#), user mentions (@), and punctuation to prepare the data for analysis.

2. Core NLP Preprocessing: Once cleaned, the text is processed using standard NLP techniques, including:

Tokenization: Splitting sentences into individual words.

Stop Word Removal: Filtering out common but non-essential words (like 'the', 'is', 'a').

Lemmatization: Reducing words to their root form (e.g., "running" becomes "run") to consolidate their meaning.

3. Feature Engineering with TF-IDF: To allow a machine learning model to understand the text, the project implements TF-IDF (Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency). This technique converts the cleaned text into a numerical matrix, giving more weight to words that are significant for determining sentiment.

4. Machine Learning Models: The system trains and compares several foundational machine learning models, including Multinomial Naive Bayes and Logistic Regression, to find the most accurate classifier for the task.

5. Performance Evaluation: The model's success isn't just measured by accuracy. The project includes a full evaluation using key metrics like Precision, Recall, F1-Score, and a Confusion Matrix to ensure the classifier is reliable and performs well for all sentiment classes (positive, negative, and neutral).
prerequisites: Willingness to learn

project_name: Citadel — Build the Algorithmic Black Box
project_description:
This project builds a fully coded miniature financial market where many autonomous trading agents interact. You create different trader types — market makers, trend followers and noise traders — and place a Reinforcement Learning agent in the center. The AI starts clueless but learns to trade by observing prices, taking risks and adapting to other agents, similar to algorithms used by top quant firms. You also build the market’s core infrastructure: an order book, trade-matching engine and simulations of supply, demand and herding behavior. The system reveals real market phenomena like bubbles, crashes and liquidity shifts. The goal is to understand how markets behave and how intelligent trading strategies emerge from simple rules.

Week 1 – Market Microstructure & System Architecture Begin with the core machinery of modern markets — order books, bid-ask spreads, liquidity depth and execution latency. You will understand how real-world exchanges function beneath the surface. You will then draft the architectural blueprint for the market simulator, dividing responsibilities across environment design, agent behavior and visualization modules. 

Week 2 – Constructing the Market Engine Develop the backbone of the project: a limit order book simulator capable of processing, queuing and matching buy–sell orders dynamically. Implement basic analytics to visualize order flow, mid-price movement and trade-level volatility in real time - essentially creating a synthetic market from scratch. 

Week 3 – Modeling Market Participants Introduce heterogeneity into the system through multiple agent archetypes - random noise traders, momentum-following speculators and liquidity-providing market makers. Fine-tune their micro-behaviors and observe how collective interactions drive emergent price formation and volatility cycles. 

Week 4 – Integrating an AI-Driven Trader Deploy a Reinforcement Learning (RL)-based trading agent using frameworks like Gymnasium and Stable-Baselines3. The AI agent interacts with the market environment, executing trades and learning from experience, rewards and competition against other agents. 

Week 5 – Emergent Market Dynamics & Behavioral Analysis Run large-scale simulations with varying agent compositions. Examine the emergence of real-world phenomena such as volatility clustering, flash crashes, bubbles, herding and liquidity traps. Analyze these through both quantitative indicators and behavioral models, bridging social learning theory with computational finance. 

Week 6 – Optimization, Insights & Demonstration Refine the AI trader through hyperparameter tuning and performance benchmarking. Visualize the evolution of its strategy, portfolio trajectory and cumulative rewards. Conclude with a demo session and research discussion - can machine intelligence uncover the same inefficiencies human traders exploit?

Expected Deliverables: A fully functional multi-agent trading simulator with a live order book and trading engine. A trained RL trading agent that interacts with other agents in the simulated market. Analytical insights and visualizations on emergent market behavior. (Optional) A research-style paper or report exploring behavioral and algorithmic phenomena observed in the simulation.

Why You Will Love It:
This project is where engineering meets Wall Street. You’ll build systems that think, simulate markets that react and witness intelligence emerge from noise. It’s a playground for coders, economists and dreamers — and a rare chance to build what real hedge funds only whisper about. By the end, you’ll have something worth showing to recruiters, professors and even potential research collaborators — a digital market where AI fights to find alpha. And yeah, all are welcome to apply :)

project_name: Mini-GPT2
project_description:
As mentors for this project, our primary goal is to guide students through the complete pipeline of natural language understanding and generation, culminating in the development and fine-tuning of a GPT-2-based model.

The work begins with a foundation in text processing techniques, including:

Tokenization – breaking text into words or subword units.

Stemming and Lemmatization – reducing words to their base or root forms to normalize language input.

Stop-word removal, case normalization, and sentence segmentation – essential preprocessing for clean and consistent data.

Word-to-Vector Representations such as Word2Vec, GloVe, and TF-IDF embeddings to convert text into numerical form suitable for modeling.

Following preprocessing, we move to document similarity and clustering:

Using cosine similarity, Euclidean distance, and Jaccard index to quantify semantic similarity between texts.

Applying dimensionality reduction techniques such as PCA (Principal Component Analysis) and t-SNE (t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding) for visualizing and clustering similar documents in lower-dimensional space.

In the advanced phase, we introduce Transformer architectures, the foundation of modern language models like GPT-2. Students learn about:

Self-attention mechanisms, positional encoding, and multi-head attention.

The concept of contextual embeddings, enabling models to understand meaning based on sentence structure.

The workflow of fine-tuning GPT-2 for domain-specific text generation tasks, along with best practices for training, validation, and evaluation.

By the end of the project, participants gain a holistic understanding of how raw text is transformed into structured data, analyzed for relationships, and ultimately used to generate coherent, context-aware text — mirroring the foundations of advanced generative AI systems.
prerequisites: Basic in python and jupyter

"Flappy Learner" is an intensive, 6-week winter project designed to guide participants through the fundamentals of Artificial Intelligence and Reinforcement Learning (RL) by building an agent that learns to play the classic game, Flappy Bird.

This project is built for accessibility, welcoming participants regardless of their prior experience. However, due to the compressed 6-week timeline, it will move at a faster pace. Week 1: Introduction to AI/ML & Essential Python Libraries (NumPy, PyTorch)

Week 2: Deep Dive into Neural Networks

Week 3: Understanding Markov Decision Processes (MDPs)

Week 4: Classic Algorithms for Solving RL Problems (e.g., Q-Learning)

project_name: FlappyBird : where Flappy learns to fly
project_description: This project trains an AI agent to play Flappy Bird game using Q-learning, a reinforcement learning technique. project_description:

project_name: Beginner's Guide to Machine Learning and Deep Learning
project_description:
This four-week intensive project is designed to take you from the fundamentals of Machine Learning (ML) to building and training your own Deep Learning (DL) models. project_name: Analysis of Geopolitical factors over Global Supply Chain using RL
project_description:
Supply chains have been studied from time immemorial, using various methodologies like operations research, game theory, process management. project_name: Accio Alpha – Kalman Filtering magic
project_description:
MAJOR OBJECTIVES:
This project is your ultimate gateway into Quantitative Finance. We will go beyond basic statistics to build, backtest, and rigorously analyze a sophisticated high-frequency trading algorithm based on the principles of mean-reversion.
The major component of this project is implementing the Kalman Filter which estimates the dynamically changing relationship between two assets, specifically the hedge ratio. You will learn to apply this state-space model, a technique widely used across finance.
You will successfully design and execute the entire algorithmic trading pipeline. This includes the initial selection of two historically co-moving assets and then code and apply the Kalman Filter for the dynamic estimation of their relationship. Following this, you will use the filter's output to define the precise entry and exit signals for trades. Finally, you will build a complete backtesting engine in Python to evaluate the strategy's performance.

KEY SKILLS YOU WILL MASTER:
This project delivers high-demand skills for careers in FinTech, Quant Research, and Data Science. You will achieve a deep understanding of Mean Reversion and Market-Neutral Strategies in finance. You will gain hands-on mastery of the Kalman Filter, a critical advanced algorithm. Your proficiency in Python (pandas/numpy) and Time-Series analysis will be significantly enhanced
prerequisites: None :) Just bring your curiosity and enthusiasm!

project_name: Kalman Filtered Trader: A RL Agent for portfolio optimization

project_name: Movie Recommendation System using Content based Filtering
project_description: This project focuses on building a Content-Based Movie Recommendation System that suggests movies similar to a selected movie by analyzing movie metadata such as genre, cast, crew, keywords, and plot overview. The system identifies patterns and relationships between movies based on their features rather than relying on user ratings or external feedback.

project_name: Blockchain-Integrated Machine learning system for Cryptocurrency Fraud Detection
project_description:
Project Overview

This project integrates machine learning and blockchain to detect and record fraudulent cryptocurrency transactions securely.
The ML component identifies abnormal transaction patterns, while blockchain ensures these predictions are immutable and transparent by storing their cryptographic hashes.
This combination enhances both intelligence and integrity — ML provides data-driven insights, and blockchain guarantees tamper-proof verification.
By the end, participants will understand how to combine data science, backend systems, and decentralized ledgers to build a real-world, verifiable fraud detection pipeline.

5-Week Plan

Week 1 – ML & Data Basics

Tech Stack

ML Tools: Pandas, Scikit-learn

Frontend (Optional): Streamlit / React, web3.py

project_name: web scraper

project_name: Sentiment Analysis for Financial News with NLP
project_description:
This project combines natural language processing (NLP) with quantitative trading, allowing you to explore how unstructured textual data (news headlines, financial reports) can be converted into tradable signals.​

The five-week structure:

Week 1: Introduction to NLP and sentiment analysis. Learn text preprocessing techniques (tokenization, stop word removal, stemming/lemmatization), and implement basic sentiment scoring using lexicon-based approaches (word counting, sentiment dictionaries).​

Week 2: Machine learning for text classification. Build a Bag-of-Words representation and train supervised learning models (Logistic Regression, Naive Bayes, K-Nearest Neighbors) on labeled financial news data to classify sentiment (positive/negative/neutral).​

Week 3: Advanced NLP with pre-trained models. Use FinBERT (a BERT model fine-tuned on financial texts) through the HuggingFace transformers library to perform sentiment analysis. Compare performance with simpler models and understand transfer learning.​

Week 4: Building trading signals from sentiment. Aggregate sentiment scores across multiple news sources, correlate sentiment with stock price movements, and develop simple trading rules (e.g., go long when sentiment improves, short when it deteriorates).​

Week 5: Backtesting the sentiment-driven strategy and evaluating performance. Analyze whether sentiment provides predictive power, investigate lag effects (how long does sentiment impact prices), and discuss market efficiency implications. Explore the theoretical ML aspects: classification accuracy, precision-recall tradeoffs, and overfitting in NLP models.
prerequisites: Basic Python programming, Basic statistics (means, probabilities),  Familiarity with machine learning concepts helpful but not required (will be introduced)

project_name: Fake News Detector using NLP

project_name: Stock Prediction model using  LSTM
project_description:
Ever wondered if machines can predict where a stock is headed next? In this project, we’ll dive into the fascinating world of stock price forecasting using Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, a powerful type of neural network that’s built to handle time-series data like stock prices.

The stock market is full of chaos, noise, and surprises and that’s exactly what makes this challenge so exciting. Our goal? To teach a model how to spot patterns in that chaos and make smart predictions based on past price movements.

We’ll start from the ground up exploring Python, data science essentials (Pandas, NumPy, Matplotlib, Scikit-learn, yfinance), and the basics of trading and technical analysis so you know what those candlesticks and indicators really mean.

Then we’ll move into hands-on modeling cleaning and preparing real stock market data, building a sliding-window dataset to capture price trends, and training our own LSTM network to forecast the next move. Along the way, you’ll tune hyperparameters, visualize predictions, and measure accuracy with metrics like MSE.

By the end, you won’t just have a working prediction model you’ll understand how data scientists and quants use machine learning to decode market behavior.

If you’ve ever wanted to mix finance, coding, and AI, this is the perfect place to start
prerequisites: none

project_name: Introduction to Anomaly Detection using Probabilistic ML
project_description:
The project aims to develop a robust and adaptive real-time anomaly detection system by integrating a hybrid suite of machine learning models. The core methodology combines probabilistic models like Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM) and Bayesian Networks for density estimation and uncertainty quantification with the fast, online learning capabilities of the Fuzzy ARTMAP neural network for adaptive pattern classification. This ensemble approach is further strengthened by incorporating non-probabilistic methods such as Isolation Forests and One-Class Support Vector Machines as baselines. 

The system architecture involves data preprocessing, multi-model training to establish "normal" baselines, an integrated anomaly detection engine that provides a consensus-based anomaly score, and a feedback loop to allow the Fuzzy ARTMAP to incrementally adapt to evolving data patterns. The expected outcome is a scalable and efficient solution capable of improving detection accuracy and reducing false positives in various applications like finance and industrial monitoring.
prerequisites: Just basics of python as well as some fundamentals of its libraries like scikit-learn , numpy , matplotlib , pandas and some basics of statistics

project_name: Predicting Market Dynamics for Data-Driven Portfolio Optimization
project_description:

project_name: Decoding the AI Black Box: Feature Visualization & Error Analysis
project_description: This project introduces the core modern concept of Deep Features (Embeddings). You will train a simple Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) on the Fashion-MNIST dataset, not just to classify, but to extract the high-dimensional feature vectors—the model's "internal thoughts." The main analytical task involves applying classical Data Science techniques like t-SNE and PCA to map these complex feature vectors into a simple, colorful 2D scatter plot. The final result will be a powerful visualization that reveals how the network organizes the data into semantic clusters. This allows you to analytically determine why the network gets confused between similar items (e.g., trousers and coats) by visually measuring the overlap in their feature space. This is a practical introduction to Model Interpretability

project_name: Augmented Reality Face Tracking and Overlay System

The system uses MediaPipe for real-time face landmark detection, OpenCV (image processing) and Pillow (image handling) to dynamically scale, position, and blend an overlay image — for example, placing sunglasses, a halo, or a crown accurately on the face. The overlay’s background is removed using rembg (AI-based background removal).

Mentees will learn how facial tracking, geometry computation, and AR rendering work together to produce effects similar to virtual try-on or face filters seen in applications like Snapchat or Lenskart. This project provides practical experience in integrating Computer Vision pipelines with Augmented Reality rendering to create real-time, face-aware visual effects.

project_name: Data-Driven Carbon Footprint Analytics for Chemical Processes
project_description: This 4-week project focuses on developing a quantitative framework to analyze and predict the carbon footprint of chemical processes using process-level operational data such as temperature, pressure, flow rate, and energy consumption. Students will perform statistical and machine learning-based modeling to identify key parameters influencing CO₂ emissions and evaluate process efficiency under different operating conditions. Alongside, a light NLP component will be used to extract sustainability targets and emission-related keywords from company sustainability reports or audit documents, allowing a comparison between reported sustainability goals and actual process data trends. By the end of the project, students will have built a data-driven emission prediction model, visualized correlations between process parameters and carbon intensity, and generated actionable insights on process optimization and sustainability alignment.
prerequisites: Basic understanding of Python and libraries like Numpy, Pandas, MatPlotlib and scikit-learn

project_name: Sarcasm Detection in News Headlines
project_description:
This project focuses on building a machine learning model that can tell whether a sentence or a news headline is sarcastic or not. For example, when someone says “I just love getting stuck in traffic”, the words sound positive, but the meaning is actually negative — that’s sarcasm! Detecting this kind of hidden meaning is tricky because it depends on understanding the context of the sentence rather than just the words themselves.

Over four weeks, one will learn how to clean and prepare text data, convert it into a form that a model can understand (using a transformer tokenizer), and fine-tune a pretrained language model to recognize sarcasm. They will train the model to classify text as sarcastic or non-sarcastic and then test how well it performs using metrics like accuracy and F1-score.

In the final week, you will also explore how to interpret the model’s predictions i.e. by seeing which words the model focuses on when it detects sarcasm. As an optional extension, you can create a simple Streamlit app where users can type in any sentence and instantly see if the model thinks it’s sarcastic or not.
prerequisites: Basic understanding of Python, Familiarity with common libraries like NumPy, Pandas, and scikit-learn

project_name: Simulation and Quantitative Analysis of the Black–Scholes Model Using Python
project_description:
This project focuses on the implementation and simulation of the Black–Scholes option pricing model, one of the foundational frameworks in quantitative finance. The objective is to understand how the model mathematically derives option prices, simulate its behavior under varying market conditions, and analyze its performance using computational techniques in Python.
The project begins by formulating the dynamics of asset prices through Geometric Brownian Motion (GBM), which models the random evolution of a stock price over time. Using Itô’s Lemma, this stochastic differential equation leads to the Black–Scholes Partial Differential Equation (PDE), from which closed-form pricing formulas for European call and put options are derived.
After establishing the mathematical foundation, the model is implemented and simulated in Python using both analytical and numerical methods:
Analytical Approach:
The closed-form Black–Scholes equations are coded to compute option prices and their sensitivities — the Greeks (Delta, Gamma, Vega, Theta, Rho). These represent how option prices react to changes in market parameters such as the underlying asset price, volatility, and time to maturity.
Monte Carlo Simulation:
To complement the analytical model, a Monte Carlo simulation is performed by generating numerous stochastic paths of the underlying asset price according to GBM dynamics. The option price is then estimated as the discounted expected payoff. This probabilistic approach not only reinforces the theoretical expectation interpretation of Black–Scholes but also allows for flexible experimentation with volatility and time parameters.
Visualization & Sensitivity Analysis:
The project employs data visualization to illustrate how option prices vary with volatility, strike price, and time to maturity. Additionally, Monte Carlo convergence plots demonstrate how simulation accuracy improves as the number of simulated paths increases.
prerequisites: Basic probability and statistics, multivariable calculus and some understanding of stochastic intuition

project_name: Bridging Language and Personalization: A Practical Dive into AI Applications
project_description:
This project delves into the depth of AI that shapes our digital lives. It begins with an understanding of the power of Large Language Models (LLMs), the foundational technology behind today's most advanced AI. From this foundation, the project explores two practical applications.

1. Sentiment Analysis crucial for algorithmically identifying and categorizing subjective information in text. Beyond just analyzing product reviews, it is essential for brand monitoring on social media, gauging public opinion, and understanding customer feedback at scale. The project explores this as a text classification problem, identifying the author's attitude—whether positive, negative, or neutral.

2. Recommender Systems, a powerful form of information filtering. The project focuses on Collaborative Filtering, a method that models preferences based on past user behavior (such as ratings or clicks) rather than item content. It operates on the user-item matrix to learn latent embeddings for both users and items. This enables effective preference elicitation and "serendipitous discovery"—suggesting relevant items a user might not have found otherwise, such as your next favorite movie or song.

The project itself is structured as a hands-on learning opportunity, welcoming anyone interested, as no prerequisites are required.
prerequisites: Knowledge of Python libraries is a plus.

project_name: Market Mood & Moves: Sentiment-Driven Stock Prediction
project_description: This project explores how collective investor sentiment—drawn from unstructured textual sources like financial news and social-media discussion—can be quantitatively analysed and used to improve stock price forecasting. Underlying the work is the behavioural finance view that markets are influenced not just by fundamentals, but by investor psychology. We will extract text data (via APIs like NewsAPI and PRAW for Reddit), apply NLP preprocessing (cleaning, tokenisation, stop-word removal, lemmatisation) and use finance-tuned deep models (e.g., FinBERT) to compute sentiment scores for each document. These scores will then be aggregated into daily sentiment signals per stock. Meanwhile we’ll pair these signals with conventional market data (returns, volume, perhaps other technical features) and build a time-series model—an LSTM network—that takes in the multi-feature sequence and predicts the next day’s return or movement direction. Finally, we translate the model’s output into trading rules (buy if up-signal, sell/short if down-signal).

project_description:
This project aims to bridge the gap between simple LLMs and true artificial reasoning. We will implement and fine-tune a specialized Large Language Model designed for complex, multi-step logical deduction, mirroring the capabilities of SOTA(State-Of-The-Art Models) like DeepSeek-R1.
Our focus is on implementing Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, not just as a prompting trick, but as a deeply embedded, fine-tuned behavior. We will begin with a high-performance base model and train it on specialized datasets to explicitly follow logical pathways.

This project is a deep dive into the complete "Reasoning Stack":

Core Fine-Tuning (SFT): We will implement Chain-of-Thought fine-tuning to teach the model to break down problems and articulate its reasoning process step-by-step.

Advanced Alignment (RL): We will go beyond basic training and apply Reinforcement Learning (specifically RLHF/DPO) to align the model's outputs, optimizing its reasoning steps for accuracy and coherence.

Agentic Integration (RAG): We will integrate our reasoning engine into an advanced RAG pipeline. Instead of just "stuffing context," our model will act as a "Reasoning Agent," capable of analyzing retrieved data, identifying contradictions, and synthesizing a final, reasoned answer.

This project is from the most widely asked domain in the internship interviews.
As an AI Researcher myself, (2 internationally published papers in the domain of AL & Quantitative Finance), I would strongly recommend this for the students thinking of pursuing their future in AI & ML.

The project uses an agentic approach. the AI not only responds to user queries but also proactively engages with the user after a few prompts to check their understanding of past topics.

The assistant maintains a structured memory of past interactions, identifies key learning points, and, after a certain interval, generates personalized recall questions. This approach reinforces long-term memory retention, mimicking how human tutors use spaced repetition to test understanding.

The system can be run as a command-line chatbot or integrated with simple front-end tools like Streamlit or Gradio for an interactive experience. It can also evaluate user responses, give feedback, and adapt its questioning style based on user performance.

project_name: TYPES OF TRESS IN DATA STRUCTURE
project_description:
This project focuses on understanding, analyzing, and visualizing various types of trees used in data structures, which are fundamental components of computer science and programming. Trees provide an efficient way to store, manage, and retrieve hierarchical data, and are widely used in databases, file systems, compilers, artificial intelligence, and more.

The project explores different tree data structures, including:

Binary Trees – where each node has at most two children.

Binary Search Trees (BSTs) – used for efficient searching, insertion, and deletion.

AVL Trees – self-balancing binary search trees that maintain height balance.

Red-Black Trees – another type of self-balancing BST used in libraries and databases.

B-Trees and B+ Trees – widely used in databases and file systems for indexing.

Heaps – complete binary trees used in priority queues and heap sort.

Trie (Prefix Tree) – used for string operations like autocomplete and spell checking.

Through this project, students can:

Learn the structure, properties, and applications of different tree types.

Understand how various tree operations (insertion, deletion, traversal, searching) are implemented.

Visualize how data is organized within each tree.

Compare performance and use cases of different tree structures.

The goal of this project is to simplify complex data structure concepts through interactive demonstrations, visual aids, and clear explanations, helping learners and developers grasp how trees optimize data processing and organization in computer systems.

project_name: Options Pricing
project_description:
In this project, we’re diving into Options Pricing using Python, taking a fresh look at the Black-Scholes Equation — the backbone of options theory. While Black-Scholes is a classic, it relies on some pretty outdated assumptions about volatility and interest rates, which don’t always hold up in today’s fast-moving markets.

To tackle this, we’ll use Deep Learning models like Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLP) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks. These models let us capture real-time market trends by using recent price and volatility data, making our predictions way more adaptive and accurate than the old-school approach. We will certainly build MLP1, MLP2, and the LSTM model, which take 20-day historical volatility as an input, while the LSTM model takes in the latest 20 days of underlying price, allowing it to learn volatility.

By the end, you’ll get hands-on with data processing and learn how to build models that go beyond Black-Scholes, blending finance and AI for modern, flexible options pricing. This project is a great way to get practical experience and add something unique to your profile.
prerequisites: There are no hard prerequisites - just bring your enthusiasm and a willingness to dive in! We’ll provide the resources and tools; your curiosity and commitment will shape how much you gain from this experience. project_name: Object Recognition System Using Deep Learning (YOLOv5 Framework)
project_description:
his project aims to design and implement an Object Recognition and Tracking System using deep learning techniques, primarily leveraging the YOLOv5 framework for object detection and the DeepSORT algorithm for object tracking in videos.

The main goal of the project is to accurately detect, classify, and continuously track multiple objects in real-time video streams. YOLOv5 (You Only Look Once, version 5) is a state-of-the-art object detection model known for its high speed and accuracy. It performs detection in a single forward pass of the network, making it ideal for real-time applications.

Once objects are detected by YOLOv5, the DeepSORT (Simple Online and Realtime Tracking with a Deep Association Metric) algorithm is used to assign unique IDs and maintain object identities across frames, even when objects overlap, move quickly, or leave and re-enter the frame. DeepSORT enhances tracking stability by combining motion information from a Kalman filter with appearance information from a deep neural network.
Through this project, participants will gain hands-on experience with real-world AI tools and workflows, learning how modern object detection and tracking systems are built and deployed.
Project Schedule:
Week 1
Basics of Neural Networks, CNNs and Open-CV
Week 2
Understanding Object Detection and YOLOV5 
Week 3
Training a YOLOV5 Model on Object images
Week 4
Using Deep-sort to utilize Trained model over video recording
prerequisites: Intermediate experience of Python and ML

project_name: DL Content Based Recommender for Movies
project_description:
This project implements a Content-Based Filtering recommender system for movies using a custom-built Deep Neural Network (DNN) architecture based on TensorFlow/Keras.

The system learns to predict a user's movie rating by generating a dense User Feature and a Movie Feature from complex, hand-engineered feature sets.
The core achievement lies in the ground-up construction and training of the dual-tower neural network model using the Keras Functional API, ensuring maximum flexibility and transparency in the feature vector generation process.
prerequisites: only python:)

project_name: From Video to Notes: Build an AI That Watches Lectures for You
project_description:
This guided project helps you create a simple AI assistant that automatically summarizes YouTube lectures into neat, readable notes. You’ll learn how to fetch transcripts using the YouTube Transcript API, process the text, and generate concise topic summaries using pre-trained transformer models like T5-small or BART.
By the end, you’ll have a working Flask or Streamlit web app that takes a YouTube link and outputs key points, timestamps, and insights. No prior AI experience required. We’ll guide you step-by-step from data extraction to model integration and front-end display.
prerequisites: Basic Python programming, Familiarity with APIs and JSON, Optional: Streamlit or Flask basics, Interest in applying AI to real-world problems, (These pre-requisites are not mandatory, they just give you a slight advantage.)

project_name: Financial Modelling
project_description:
Ever wondered how analysts on Wall Street decide what a company is really worth? Or how spreadsheets can tell the story of an entire business?
In this project, you’ll step into the shoes of a financial analyst -> building real, dynamic models from scratch. From decoding financial statements to predicting future profits and valuing companies, this project blends finance, logic, and data science into one exciting winter adventure.

By the end, you’ll not only know your way around Excel like a pro, but also use Python to make your models smarter, faster, and way cooler.


• What You’ll Learn

The language of finance — income statements, balance sheets, and cash flows.

How to build and link these into a 3-statement model.

How to value companies using Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) and relative valuation.

How to stress-test assumptions through scenario and sensitivity analysis.

How to use Python to supercharge financial analysis and visualize results
.

• 4-Week Adventure Plan

Week	Theme	What You’ll Do	Milestone

1. Decode the Numbers	Learn to read, interpret, and link financial statements.	Build your first 3-statement model (IS, BS, CF).	
2. The Valuation Toolkit	Create ratio dashboards and forecast future performance.	Compute WACC and set up your DCF base model.	
3. The Analyst’s Playground	Extend DCF, try out relative valuation, and test scenarios.	Complete your full-fledged valuation model.	
4. Python x Finance	Use Python to automate calculations and visualize valuation insights.	Submit your final model + analytical report.
	

• How We’ll Roll

1. Learn the Basics — simple intros to finance, valuation, and Excel magic.


2. Build Your Model — real company data, hands-on spreadsheets.


3. Add the Data-Science Twist — a dash of Python for smart analytics.


4. Showcase Your Work — report, insights, and models that tell a story.


• Skills You’ll Pick Up

Financial statement analysis

Excel modelling and linking

Company valuation (DCF & multiples)

Python for finance (pandas, NumPy, matplotlib)

Data storytelling and report writing


• Resources You’ll Love

Books: Pignataro’s Financial Modeling and Valuation, Rosenbaum & Pearl’s Investment Banking

Courses: Aswath Damodaran’s Valuation lectures (YouTube), CFI/Wall Street Prep modules

Tools: Excel, Python


• What You’ll Deliver

A working Excel + Python financial model

A concise report explaining your logic and results

A serious boost to your data-driven finance portfolio


• Duration

4 Weeks (During WiDS 2025) — individual project
prerequisites: Just lots of enthu and Interest in finance

project_name: Spotify Song Mood Classifier
project_description:
Music is emotional every song carries a distinct mood, from energetic and happy to calm or melancholic.
The Spotify Song Mood Classifier is an AI project that aims to predict a song’s mood using its audio features such as tempo, energy, valence, danceability, and acousticness.

Using publicly available Spotify datasets (or the Spotify API), this project guides you through every step of the data-science pipeline from Python programming and exploratory analysis to model building and visualization.
By the end, you’ll have a working model  and possibly a small web app that classifies songs by mood and can even recommend “vibe-based” playlists.

Week wise plan -
Week 1 – Python & Data Foundations:
Learn Python basics and explore the Spotify dataset using pandas and matplotlib.

Week 2 – Exploratory Data Analysis:
Understand Spotify audio features, clean the data, and discover patterns linking sound attributes to mood.

Week 3 – Model Building:
Train your first machine-learning model to classify songs into mood categories.

Week 4 – Model Optimization & Insights:
Refine the model, analyze feature importance, and visualize how musical traits influence emotion.

Week 5 – Visualization & Deployment:
Build an interactive Streamlit app and present your final mood classification results with visuals and insights.
prerequisites: Only your enthusiasm

project_name: GPU Programming using CUDA and Triton
project_description:
This winter project offers a hands-on, 6-week guided learning path inspired by NVIDIA’s internal CUDA engineer training roadmap. Participants will go beyond tutorials to develop deep intuition about GPU hardware, parallel programming, and memory optimization.

Week 1 — GPU Intuition & Hardware Foundations
Understand how GPUs differ from CPUs and why they excel at parallel workloads.

Week 2 — Parallel Thinking & Algorithm Design
Learn to design algorithms that map efficiently to GPU architectures.

Week 3 — CUDA Fundamentals
Write your first CUDA kernels and experiment with threads, blocks, and grids.

Week 4 — Memory Optimization
Master GPU memory hierarchy and implement shared memory optimizations.

Week 5 — Real Kernels
Build and benchmark real-world kernels like Softmax and matrix multiplication.

Week 6 — Triton for Modern GPU Programming
Use OpenAI’s Triton to write high-performance kernels with concise, Pythonic syntax.
prerequisites: Python, Linear Algebra, Basic knowledge of processor design will help but is not necessary

project_name: Auto-Damage Vision
project_description: This project focuses on building an automated system that detects visible damage on vehicles using computer vision techniques. The goal is to classify whether a given vehicle is damaged or not damaged and classify the severity of the damage, and optionally highlight the damaged region. This simulates real-world applications in insurance claims, garage automation, and fleet management.
prerequisites: Fundamental python required to understand depth and a little bit of basics of ML preferred

project_name: Equity classification using Machine Learning on Financial Ratios
project_description: Project: Building a classifier on the fundamental financial ratios of an equity (as opposed to stock prices), to predict the investment decision for the equity. Note - We will only deal with long term outcomes of these investments as opposed to prediction of short term fluctuations which is the domain of algorithmic trading. You will: - Build models of multiple types with varying hyper-parameters. - Interpret and compare the results of different models and its implications on the classification problem at hand - Compare the ML predictions to the conventional method of equity selection and its implications on the classification problem at hand. Key takeaways: - What are financial ratios and how are the conventionally used in equity selection? - Execution of various models (decision trees, LDA, NN, etc.) and best practices in dealing with data. - Interpretation of machine learning models in a field relevant manner.
prerequisites: Python experience

project_name: VisionLock - Build a Facial Recognition Tool
project_description: In this project, mentees will build a facial recognition system using deep learning. They’ll start with face detection and alignment using OpenCV/MTCNN, extract feature embeddings with models like FaceNet or Siamese Networks, and implement similarity-based verification for identity matching. By the end, participants will have hands-on experience in computer vision, transfer learning, and real-time face recognition using a live webcam interface.
prerequisites: All one needs is enthusiasm! Knowing a bit of NumPy, Pandas, or TensorFlow/PyTorch is a bonus.

project_name: Financial Analysis of Multiple Models used in Corporate Finance and Economics
project_description: This project explores a broad range of analytical models commonly used in corporate finance and economics. The goal is to understand how these models work, compare their assumptions, evaluate their real-world applications, and identify their strengths and limitations. The project will be divided into multiple subtopics, each focusing on a specific financial or economic model. Examples include valuation models (DCF, comparables), capital structure theories (Modigliani–Miller, trade-off theory), risk and return models (CAPM, APT), forecasting models, macroeconomic frameworks, and more. Through detailed analysis, simulations, case studies, and comparative evaluations, this project aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of how these models support decision-making in corporate finance and economic policy. It is designed to help students and practitioners deepen their knowledge, develop analytical skills, and gain practical insights into the tools used in financial and economic analysis.
prerequisites: None

project_name: Noisy Truth
project_description: 👋 Welcome to "Noisy Truth"! Ever wonder how a self-driving car or a deep-sea sub knows exactly where it is without GPS? They use a powerful trick to fuse messy, unreliable sensor data into one clear, high-confidence "truth." In this project, you'll learn that trick. We'll start with the classic Kalman Filter, but our main mission is to build the Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF)—the "pro-level" upgrade for handling the real world's complex, curvy paths. Our core challenge: We'll build the "brain" for an Autonomous Underwater Vehicle (AUV). We'll have to take its wildly drifting internal sensors and combine them with fuzzy, noisy sonar "pings" to find its true path in the dark. By the end, you'll have mastered a core skill used in robotics, aerospace, and beyond: the ability to find truth in the noise.
prerequisites: basic python

project_name: Predictive Customer Analytics: CLV Forecasting & Behavioral Segmentation Using RFM Methodology
project_description: This project is a focused 6-week intermediate-level analytics initiative where you will learn to build a predictive system that forecasts customer lifetime value (CLV) and segments customers using Recency, Frequency, Monetary (RFM) analysis. Starting with cleaning and exploring real customer transaction data, you will engage in feature engineering to create meaningful variables reflecting customer behavior, purchase patterns, and engagement. Using RFM methodology, you will segment customers into actionable groups that inform targeted marketing strategies. Then, you’ll build machine learning models (logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost) to predict customer churn with high precision and recall, helping identify customers at risk of leaving. Parallelly, you will calculate and model CLV to estimate each customer’s projected revenue contribution, enabling smarter budget allocation. By project end, you’ll have honed skills in Python programming, data analysis, machine learning, business intelligence, and storytelling—empowering you to translate data into actionable business decisions as done by leading companies worldwide
prerequisites: Proficiency in Python, along with its core data science libraries like pandas, numpy, scikit-learn, and matplotlib.

project_name: ML Meets the Sun and Wind: Smart Mapping for Renewable Energy Hotspots
project_description: Imagine teaching AI to “hunt for sunshine and wind” from space 🌤️! In this project, you’ll harness the power of Remote Sensing, Machine Learning, and Geospatial Intelligence to find the perfect spots for solar panels and wind turbines. Using data from satellites like Sentinel, ERA5, and NASA POWER, you’ll build a smart model that blends terrain analysis, solar irradiance, wind velocity, and land use patterns into one AI-driven energy suitability map. From coding in Python and Google Earth Engine to generating dazzling heatmaps of renewable potential, you’ll get to see data science light up the future of sustainable energy. 🌞⚙️💡 This will help you understand how energy systems, sustainability and GIS intersect with ML and you'll have a cool inter-disciplinary project to showcase at the end of this !! Week 3: Convert raw satellite data into usable features for ML and understand various models + Teach your ML model what “good” energy sites look like Week 4: Create cool maps on GEE or QGIS + Validate your Models Week 5: Interact with peers, showcase your models and refine based on feedback Week 6: Final Project Report writing/ Presentation

project_name: AI Media Automation Lab
project_description: This is a collaborative mentorship initiative where participants learn to design and build fully autonomous AI pipelines that transform real-time data—like news, trends, or ideas—into complete, publish-ready video content. Through hands-on projects, mentees explore how to combine large language models (LLMs), intelligent agents, text-to-speech systems, and automated video generation tools to create dynamic media experiences. This program covers every layer of modern AI automation: from prompt engineering, data parsing, and multimodal reasoning, to voice synthesis, visual composition, and social media distribution. By the end, mentees will have built a real-world system capable of fetching information, generating creative scripts, producing videos with AI voices and visuals, and auto-publishing them—an end-to-end learning journey that blends technical depth with creative storytelling.

project_name: Minigames using SAT solver
project_description: In this project we will look at how SAT solvers can be used to solve small logic puzzles. We start by learning the basics of propositional logic—how to write simple true/false statements and combine them to express rules. After that, we introduce the main ideas behind DPLL, the basic procedure used by many SAT solvers to search for a solution. Using these ideas, the project focuses on turning games like Sudoku and Tsukoban into sets of logical rules and using a SAT solver to automatically find solutions.
prerequisites: None :) Just bring your curiosity and enthusiasm!

project_name: OncoNet - Skin Cancer Classification and Lesion Segmentation Using Deep Learning and Vision Transformers
project_description:
This project focuses on developing an advanced, end-to-end artificial intelligence system capable of accurately detecting and analyzing skin cancer using dermoscopic medical images. Leveraging the internationally recognized ISIC (International Skin Imaging Collaboration) datasets, participants will work with one of the world’s largest and most reliable open repositories of skin lesion images, widely used in medical research and global diagnostic challenges.

The objective of the project is twofold. First, students will build a multi-class skin cancer classification model that can distinguish between several clinically recognized skin lesion types, including melanoma, basal cell carcinoma, benign keratosis, and others. This task will involve constructing baseline convolutional neural network (CNN) models, progressing to more sophisticated architectures such as EfficientNet and modern Vision Transformers (ViT). This progression will provide a strong understanding of both classical deep learning and contemporary transformer-based approaches for image analysis.

Second, participants will develop a lesion segmentation model that precisely identifies the boundaries of skin abnormalities in the images. This portion of the project will utilize U-Net and its advanced variants, enabling pixel-level segmentation of the lesion area. The segmentation component is critical for medical applications, as it supports explainability, enhances diagnostic accuracy, and mirrors the structure of professional medical imaging competitions such as the ISIC Challenge. For advanced learners, the project can be extended to incorporate Transformer-based segmentation models such as TransUNet.

Beyond building predictive models, students will learn essential medical AI practices, including proper dataset preprocessing, class imbalance handling, rigorous evaluation using metrics such as AUC, F1-score, Dice coefficient, and Intersection over Union, and generation of clinically interpretable visual explanations. Techniques like Grad-CAM and attention map visualization from Vision Transformers will be used to provide insight into model decisions, aligning with standards expected in medical research settings.

By the end of the program, participants will have constructed a complete medical imaging pipeline that integrates classification, segmentation, and interpretability—skills directly relevant to cutting-edge research and competitions in medical AI.
prerequisites: Basic Python programming and familiarity with NumPy, Pandas, and Matplotlib. Prior exposure to machine learning concepts is helpful but not required, as all essential ML and deep learning foundations will be learnt during the project.

project_name: Battery SOH estimation
mentor_name: Aditya O, Harshvardhan Srivastav and Aryaman Kavi
project_description:
This intensive winter course explores the intersection of computational physics and deep learning, specifically focusing on Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs). Students will address a critical challenge in the renewable energy sector: estimating the State of Health (SOH) of Lithium-ion batteries.

Unlike traditional data-driven approaches that treat physical systems as "black boxes," this course teaches a hybrid methodology. Students will integrate the governing partial differential equations (PDEs) of electrochemistry directly into neural network loss functions, creating models that are robust, data-efficient, and physically consistent. By the conclusion of the course, participants will have developed a functional "Digital Twin" capable of estimating battery degradation parameters from standard voltage and current measurement
prerequisites: Python (Intermediate: NumPy, PyTorch/TensorFlow basics),  Calculus (Basic understanding of derivatives/gradients).
